question: Did the early Church accept slavery?

answers.label: It accepted slavery as a fact but changed how slaves were treated
Slaves and masters were equal brothers in Christ
Owning human beings is a sin

overview.text: The early Church did not try to abolish slavery. Ignatius tells masters not to be proud, and slaves not to expect the church to buy their freedom, which shows some churches did.
Inside the Church, slaves and free were "brothers" (Minucius Felix), and a former slave could become bishop of Rome.
Gregory of Nyssa, about 379, condemned owning human beings outright: for how many coins did you buy the image of God? He was almost alone in the ancient world.

Lactantius says Christians have no slaves but call them brothers in spirit and fellow slaves in religion. Chrysostom urges the rich, if they truly care for slaves, to buy them, teach them a trade and set them free, yet he still allows a master one or two servants. The pattern remains brotherhood and regulation, not abolition, Gregory of Nyssa alone excepted.

quotes.author: Ignatius of Antioch
quotes.english: Do not be haughty toward slaves, male or female; but neither let them be puffed up. Let them serve all the more for the glory of God, so that they may obtain a better freedom from God. Let them not desire to be set free at the common expense, so that they may not be found slaves of desire.
quotes.original: δούλους καὶ δούλας μὴ ὑπερηφάνει: ἀλλὰ μηδὲ αὐτοὶ φυσιούσθωσαν, ἀλλ’ εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ πλέον δουλευέτωσαν, ἵνα κρείττονος ἐλευθερίας ἀπὸ θεοῦ τύχωσιν. μὴ ἐράτωσαν ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ ἐλευθεροῦσθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοῦλοι εὑρεθῶσιν ἐπιθυμίας.
quotes.context: "At the common expense" shows that churches sometimes paid to free slaves. Ignatius discourages slaves from expecting it.

quotes.author: Minucius Felix
quotes.english: So we love one another with mutual love, which you resent, since we do not know how to hate; so we call one another brothers, which you envy, as children of one God and Father.
quotes.original: sic mutuo, quod doletis, amore diligimus, quoniam odisse non novimus: sic nos, quod invidetis, fratres vocamus, ut unius Dei parentis
quotes.context: Masters and slaves alike were "brothers" in the Church. Callistus, a former slave, became bishop of Rome about 217.

quotes.author: Lactantius
quotes.english: And there is no other reason why we give one another the name of brothers, except that we believe we are equals. For since we measure all human things not by the body but by the spirit, although the condition of bodies is different, we nevertheless have no slaves, but we both regard and call them brothers in spirit, fellow slaves in religion.
quotes.original: nec alia causa est cur nobis inuicem fratrum nomen inpertiamus, nisi quia pares esse nos credimus. nam cum omnia humana non corpore, sed spiritu metiamur, tametsi corporum sit diuersa condicio, nobis tamen serui non sunt, sed eos et habemus et dicimus spiritu fratres, religione conseruos.
quotes.context: Lactantius answers an imagined objector who points to rich and poor, slaves and masters among Christians. He does not claim the legal institution had disappeared; his claim is how Christians regard and name one another.

quotes.author: Gregory of Nyssa
quotes.english: "I got me slaves and slave girls" (Ecclesiastes 2:7). What do you mean? You condemn to slavery a human being, whose nature is free and self-governing, and you make laws against God, overturning his law for nature. ... "I got me slaves and slave girls." For what price, tell me? What did you find among existing things worth as much as this nature? For how many obols did you value the image of God? For how many staters did you sell the nature God shaped? ... Only God could do this; or rather, not even God himself.
quotes.original: Ἐκτησάμην δούλους καὶ παιδίσκας. τί λέγεις; δουλείᾳ καταδικάζεις τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οὗ ἐλευθέρα ἡ φύσις καὶ αὐτεξού σιος, καὶ ἀντινομοθετεῖς τῷ θεῷ, ἀνατρέπων αὐτοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ τῇ ... Ἐκτησάμην γὰρ δούλους καὶ παιδίσκας. ποίας, εἰπέ μοι, τιμῆς; τί εὗρες ἐν τοῖς οὖσι τῆς φύσεως ταύτης ἀντάξιον; πόσου κέρματος ἐτιμήσω τὸν λόγον; πόσοις ὀβολοῖς τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ θεοῦ ἀντεστάθμησας; πόσων στατήρων τὴν θεόπλαστον φύσιν ἀπενεπόλησας; ... μόνου θεοῦ τὸ δυνηθῆναι τοῦτο, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδὲ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ.
quotes.context: A Lenten sermon about 379. It is the only surviving ancient text that condemns slave-owning itself, not just its abuses.

quotes.author: John Chrysostom
quotes.english: The race of slaves was not brought in for any need, since a slave would have been created along with Adam if it had been; it is the penalty of sin and the punishment of disobedience. ... So it is not necessary to own a slave; if it is necessary at all, let it be only one, or at most a second. ... For if you really cared for them, you would not keep anyone busy in your service, but would buy them, teach them trades so that they can support themselves, and let them go free.
quotes.original: Οὐδὲ γὰρ χρείας ἕνεκεν τὸ τῶν δούλων ἐπεισήχθη γένος, ἐπεὶ μετὰ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ ἐπλάσθη ἂν καὶ δοῦλος· ἀλλ’ ἁμαρτίας ἐστὶ τὸ ἐπιτίμιον, καὶ τῆς παρακοῆς ἡ κόλασις. ... Ὥστε οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον τὸ δοῦλον ἔχειν· εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀναγκαῖον, ἕνα που μόνον, ἢ τὸ πολὺ δεύτερον. ... ἐπεὶ, εἰ κηδόμενος, μηδένα εἰς διακονίαν ἀπασχολήσῃς τὴν σὴν, ἀλλ’ ἀγοράσας, καὶ τέχνας διδάξας ὥστε ἀρκεῖν ἑαυτοῖς, ἄφες ἐλευθέρους.
quotes.context: From the moral exhortation (section 5) of Homily 40 on 1 Corinthians, against keeping retinues of household slaves for show. Chrysostom still permits one or two servants and treats slavery as a penalty for sin; his counsel to buy in order to teach and free goes beyond mere regulation, but it is not a call to abolish the institution.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: This name was earned by guilt, not by nature. The origin of the word servi (slaves) in the Latin language is believed to be derived from this: those who could by the law of war have been killed were kept alive by the victors and became slaves (servi), named from being spared (a servando). The first cause of slavery, then, is sin, by which man was subjected to man by the bond of a shared condition; this does not happen except by God's judgment, with whom there is no injustice, and who knows how to distribute different punishments according to the merits of offenders. But no one, by the nature in which God first created man, is a slave either of man or of sin.
quotes.original: Nomen itaque istud culpa meruit, non natura. Origo autem uocabuli seruorum in Latina lingua inde creditur ducta, quod hi, qui iure belli possent occidi, a uictoribus cum seruabantur serui fiebant, a seruando appellati ... Prima ergo seruitutis causa peccatum est, ut homo homini condicionis uinculo subderetur; quod non fit nisi Deo iudicante, apud quem non est iniquitas et nouit diuersas poenas meritis distribuere delinquentium. ... Nullus autem natura, in qua prius Deus hominem condidit, seruus est hominis aut peccati.
quotes.context: Augustine denies that slavery is natural, against Aristotle: he treats it as a penal consequence of sin, imposed under God's just judgment, and he does not call for its abolition. The name servus, he says, preserves the memory that war captives who might lawfully have been killed were spared instead.

method: Every early quote was read in its Greek or Latin and translated for this page by Claude (Opus 5.5) on 13 October 2026. Each line names the printed edition it was read from.
